THE MAINE SENATE

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and honorable members of the Education and Cultural
Affairs,
My name is Mike Tipping. I represent Senate District 8 in Penobscot County and I'm proud to present LD 1071, Resolve, Directing the Department of Education to Conduct a Review of
the Implementation of Public Law 2021, Chapter 295 and Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Consult with School Administrators Regarding Developing
a Plan for Community-based Crisis Receiving Centers.

I submitted this bill last year after meeting with school administrators, teachers and parents in
Lincoln following a series of recent bomb threats made at the local junior high school, as well as
several student deaths at the high school.

It would take two important steps to address student safety and mental health support for

schools:

.

First, it would direct the Department of Education to conduct a review of the implementation of
Public Law 2021 Chapter 295 and options for behavioral response for students who have
recently made a threat of bodily harm but don't currently pose an imminent danger of serious
physical injury.
Right now, many school districts, including RSU 67 in the Lincoln Lakes region, believe that
This law restricts their ability to remove students who have made a threat from the classroom. In
speaking with representatives of the Department of Eduction, they believe these options are not
so limited, but representatives of the Maine School Management Association report that other school districts have the same impression.

I hope this is simply a misunderstanding that a review and some additional communication can
address.

I have two 11-year old kids, exactly the age that the law limiting suspensions and expulsions
addresses. I know that they aren't at an age where these punishments are helpful to their development, but I also know that they shouldn't have to try to learn while sitting next to a student who made a violent threat the day before.
Second, this bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services, while developing a plan for a network of community-based crisis receiving centers as required by Public Law 2024

Current law requires these crisi receiving centers work with a variety of local stakeholders, but

I appreciate your consideration and I'd be happy to answer any questions.

Senator Rafferty, Chair Representative Noonan-Murphy, Chair Members, Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0100

Re: LD 1071 - Resolve, Directing the Department of Education to Conduct a Review of the Implementation of Public Law 2021, Chapter 295 and Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Consult with School Administrators Regarding Developing a Plan for Community-based Crisis Receiving Centers

Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan-Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition to LD 1071, Resolve, Directing the Department of Education to Conduct a Review of the Implementation of Public Law 2021, Chapter 295 and Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Consult with School Administrators Regarding Developing a Plan for Community-based Crisis Receiving Centers.

The intent of this resolve is to direct the Department of Education to conduct a review of the implementation of Public Law 2021, chapter 295, and options for disciplinary response for students who have recently made a threat of bodily harm but do not currently pose an imminent danger of serious bodily injury. This resolve would also require the Department of Health and Human Services to consult with school administrators to examine how community-based crisis receiving centers may be integrated with school mental health and substance use disorder response services, providing a report regarding its findings to the Joint Standing Committee by December 3, 2025. While the Office of Behavioral Health (OBH) is fully supportive of expanded access to crisis services and coordination within school systems, this bill doesn't acknowledge or reference the ongoing and comprehensive work and services offered within the existing crisis continuum in Maine.

As drafted, LD 1071 proposes a duplication of current efforts that the Department is involved in related to the modernization and expansion of the crisis continuum, and individual services within the continuum. If this legislation were to move forward, it may have the unintended consequence of complicating, slowing down, and impeding the crisis system reform work that is already underway.

OBH is open to educating and consulting with schools regarding the current crisis continuum and services offered, including education around crisis receiving centers. Currently, there is just one Crisis Receiving Center in Maine, operated by Spurwink in Cumberland County. While the Department is working towards the development of a Crisis Receiving Center network, with an

open RFP for services in Penobscot and Androscoggin Counties, these other receiving centers will not be operational by the time this report will be due to the Legislature, limiting the ability to gather and provide data to the Committee. It is also important to note that Crisis Receiving Centers only serve ages 14+ and they do not offer telehealth services, which would require schools to transport appropriately aged youth to Crisis Receiving Centers. Further, OBH would like to highlight that a Crisis Receiving Center is only one piece of a best-practice crisis response continuum that includes: Someone to Call, Someone to Respond, and Somewhere to Go; OBH recommends that the Department of Education and local school units consider all parts of the continuum in its youth crisis response. A pediatric urgent care model is currently being piloted through Certified Community Behavioral Health Center (CCBHC) implementation, and this model would be an appropriate vessel to accomplish the intended goal of this legislation.
It should also be noted that there were an estimated 3,200 contacts to Maine's crisis hotlines for children in crisis who were referred to a mobile crisis response in SFY 2024. Of those approximately 3,200 contacts, it is estimated that around 20% of those contacts were initiated by schools on behalf of a child in crisis. There were also approximately 8,500 initial mobile crisis encounters reported in SFY 2024, of which an estimated 32% were for children in crisis. These data points are provided to highlight the ways in which children are already been served by the Crisis Continuum in Maine.
For these reasons, OBH does not feel that a legislative resolve is required for the Department to continue this work as it is already being integrated into everyday practice.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Sarah Squirrell Director Office of Behavioral Health Maine Department of Health and Human Services
